edges.description: Cortisol production that no longer depends on pituitary ACTH is the clinical syndrome the autonomous adrenocortical nodules produce.
Autonomous expression of the steroidogenic machinery in the nodular cortex raises circulating cortisol independently of ACTH drive.
Deregulated differentiation and proliferation of adrenocortical cells produce the small pigmented micronodules that define the histopathology.
Cortisol produced autonomously by the adrenal nodules is accompanied by suppressed rather than raised corticotropin, which is the biochemical pattern reported in genetically confirmed PPNAD.

nodes.description: Constitutive PKA activity drives autonomous, ACTH-independent expression of steroidogenic genes and cortisol production, together with deregulated adrenocortical cell differentiation and increased proliferation, yielding bilateral micronodular hyperplasia. The adrenal-cortex-specific Prkar1a knockout mouse recapitulates pituitary-independent Cushing syndrome and bilateral hyperplasia, demonstrating that RIalpha loss is sufficient. Transcriptomic studies show increased expression of steroidogenic acute regulatory protein and the steroidogenic enzymes CYP17A1 and CYP21A2.

nodes.description: PRKAR1A-mutant adrenocortical tissue shows enhanced MAPK signaling, with increased phosphorylated ERK1/2, B-raf, phospho-MEK1/2, and phospho-c-Myc. These changes are proposed to provide proliferative signals contributing to nodule formation. Comparative whole-genome expression profiling further shows overexpression of Wnt pathway genes (CCND1, CTNNB1, LEF1, LRP5, WISP1, WNT3) in PRKAR1A-mutant lesions, linking cAMP/PKA activation to Wnt-driven proliferative programs.

nodes.description: Constitutional duplication or amplification of PRKACA, the gene encoding the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A, is a distinct germline lesion from PRKAR1A loss: the catalytic subunit is gained rather than the regulatory subunit lost, and the reported cases are attributed to constitutive activation of that catalytic subunit. Systematic screening of 781 bilateral nodular adrenocortical disease index cases found PRKACA duplication only in patients whose pathology was PPNAD, and the duplication generates topologically associated neo-domains in tumour Hi-C maps.

nodes.description: Germline inactivating variants in PRKAR1A reduce or eliminate the type I alpha regulatory subunit (RIalpha) of protein kinase A. Loss of regulatory restraint releases the PKA catalytic subunits, producing increased cAMP-stimulated catalytic kinase activity in adrenocortical cells. Many PRKAR1A variants are premature stop codons triggering nonsense-mediated decay and haploinsufficiency, with up-regulation of other PKA subunits.

nodes.description: Germline reduced-function variants in the phosphodiesterases PDE11A and PDE8B impair cAMP degradation, and this is the second route into the same autonomous steroidogenic programme that PRKAR1A loss and PRKACA gain reach, with no lesion in either of those genes. PDE8B is cAMP-specific. Both genes were first linked to isolated micronodular adrenocortical disease, and MONDO files them as the PPNAD2 and PPNAD3 children of this entry's own term. The two are not equivalent in strength of evidence: inactivating PDE11A defects were described as low-penetrance predisposing factors, consistent with PDE11A variants frequently co-occurring with PRKAR1A variants in PPNAD cohorts, whereas the reported PDE8B mutation was shown to measurably alter the protein's cAMP-degrading capacity in vitro.

nodes.description: PKA activates the mTOR pathway in adrenocortical cells, and this contributes in vivo to resistance to apoptosis in PPNAD, allowing accumulation of autonomously functioning nodular cells. Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin restored apoptosis sensitivity in the Prkar1a knockout mouse model, nominating mTORC1 as a candidate therapeutic target.
